10fc1751-c3af-529f-8796-f8e46bfb1691: Read each letter name, then join them into one word: H-A-L-L-O spells **Hallo**. Note the double **L**.
extra-a11-l01-01: Every German letter has its own name. The letter Z is called **Zett** — not "zed" or "zee".
dfa7474b-af31-5c93-8031-0bb797360123: Join the letters into one word: T-S-C-H-Ü-S-S spells **Tschüss**. The **Ü** is u-Umlaut, and the word ends in double **S**.

d662cf8b-e87f-5b87-8370-2b0e0feff300: Join the letters into one word: D-A-N-K-E spells **Danke** (thank you). Five letters, no double letters.

2488cb0f-ea25-5dae-85d8-fea6ed13b2f3: Join the letters into one word: E-N-T-S-C-H-U-L-D-I-G-U-N-G spells **Entschuldigung** (excuse me). Long word, 14 letters — read slowly.

448a9516-9d53-5c58-8f77-9ae1e60d9363: Join the letters into one word: G-R-U-ß spells **Gruß** (greeting). The last letter is **ß** (Eszett), not double s.
9d61145f-8a24-5b5a-85e3-6cb9dfc99315: Join the letters into one word: H-E-I-ß-E-N spells **heißen** (to be called). It is a verb, so it starts lowercase, and it contains **ß**.
8bb13847-96f2-5671-8c3e-a8e40d6ad1eb: Join the letters into one word: B-U-C-H-S-T-A-B-I-E-R-E-N spells **buchstabieren** (to spell). A verb, so lowercase; 13 letters.
extra-a11-l01-09: The morning greeting is the fixed phrase **Guten Morgen**. The form is **Guten** with -n, and both words together.
1d19c92e-e77d-5f3f-8e68-0cfd0223e650: Join the letters into one word: B-U-C-H-S-T-A-B-E spells **Buchstabe** (letter). A noun, so it starts with a capital letter.

9f22442a-a212-57af-8f9f-fd3c30231a4e: Join the letters into one word: V-O-R-N-A-M-E spells **Vorname** (first name). The first letter is **V** (Vau), not W.
3befc1a5-09d9-5c0e-8f59-67c00b247ffa: Join the letters into one word: N-A-C-H-N-A-M-E spells **Nachname** (last name). Eight letters, no double letters.
85386a42-7cb4-5293-8a1b-fb8a5bb8e494: The letter ß is called **Eszett** (also "scharfes S"). The question asks for the letter's name, not its sound.
eb59458f-62a5-539c-805e-5e94744b68cc: The letter Y is called **Ypsilon** in German. The question asks for the name of the letter, not its sound.
23520fbd-d64b-5992-838d-6c6f27c7e999: The letter J is called **Jot** in German. Be careful: G is "ge" and J is **Jot** — an easy pair to mix up.
ff1f6816-195c-5bf3-846d-9f904ef8c7cd: The letter V is called **Vau** in German. Do not confuse it with W, which is called "we".
559f4c15-815e-5d09-8929-f19548ef12cb: The letter Z is called **Zett** in German — not "zed" or "zee" as in English.
0eb1a415-1bd6-5983-8951-b33d16ebb054: B-E-R-U-F spells Beruf (job). Learn every noun with its article: it is **der Beruf** (masculine).
74f91cf4-e8b5-5ee1-887a-84e6370ac670: A-D-R-E-S-S-E spells Adresse (address). Learn the noun together with its article: **die Adresse** (feminine).
92ac55de-fb60-5f58-8698-7e85444b2255: T-E-L-E-F-O-N-N-U-M-M-E-R spells Telefonnummer (phone number). Its article is feminine: **die Telefonnummer**. Note the double **N** and double **M**.
cbee2a2c-2b4a-5d9b-88d1-1b5bc64f3294: F-O-R-M-U-L-A-R spells Formular (form). Its article is neuter: **das Formular**. Learn noun and article as one unit.
32eb463d-1209-5db8-8aee-d227e1d99d62: W-O-H-N-O-R-T spells Wohnort (place of residence). Its article is masculine: **der Wohnort**. Learn noun and article together.
2df8b952-57b5-54ef-8c10-4a0d965d9115: The correct spelling is **Danke**: D-A-N-K-E. The wrong options drop a letter ("Dane") or swap two letters ("Dnake").
87e8f16d-a3fa-5012-8d47-373e6b16f736: The correct spelling is **Vorname**: V-O-R-N-A-M-E. The other options swap letters ("Vonrame") or leave one out ("Vornae").
b08c9136-4135-57f2-89d8-c1eabb28ef77: The correct spelling is **Telefonnummer**, with double **N** and double **M**. The distractors drop a letter or scramble the order.
extra-a11-l01-11: When spelling, say each letter separately: **D-A-N-K-E**. Five letters, no double letters.
extra-a11-l01-12: Spelling means saying every letter one by one: **E-N-T-S-C-H-U-L-D-I-G-U-N-G**. Take it slowly — 14 letters.
extra-a11-l01-13: Spell letter by letter: **B-I-T-T-E**. The word has a double **T**, so you say T twice.
extra-a11-l01-14: Spell letter by letter: **W-I-L-L-K-O-M-M-E-N**. Two double letters — say **L** twice and **M** twice.
extra-a11-l01-15: The evening greeting is the fixed phrase **Guten Abend**. It follows the same pattern as Guten Morgen and Guten Tag.
extra-a11-l01-16: The greeting is a fixed phrase: **Guten Morgen**, always with **-n**. "Gute Morgen" is the common mistake.
extra-a11-l01-17: The greeting is a fixed phrase: **Guten Abend**, always with **-n**. "Gute Abend" is wrong.
extra-a11-l01-20: **Zett** is the German name of the letter **Z**. Learn the names so you can spell aloud.
extra-a11-l01-21: **Ypsilon** is the German name of the letter **Y**. It sounds nothing like the English letter name.
extra-a11-l01-22: **Eszett** is the German name of the letter **ß** (sharp s). It only exists in German.
extra-a11-l01-03: The letter ß has its own name: **Eszett**, also called **scharfes S**. Never spell it as "double s".
extra-a11-l01-06: When you talk to Frau Kaya, you use the formal you (Sie). The formal phrase is **Wie geht es Ihnen?** — with a capital **I**.
extra-a11-l01-07: The verb heißen (to be called) after **ich** takes the ending **-e**: **Ich heiße Ana.** The subject comes first, the verb second.
extra-a11-l01-08: The greeting is a fixed phrase: **Guten Tag**, always with **-n**. "Gute Tag" is the common mistake.

extra-a11-l01-19: The polite question to someone you address formally (Sie) is the fixed phrase **Wie geht es Ihnen?** — with a capital **I**.
extra-a11-l01-23: Subject first, verb second. After **ich** the verb ends in **-e**: **Ich buchstabiere Ana.**
extra-a11-l01-24: To a friend (informal you, du) the question is the fixed phrase **Wie geht es dir?** To Frau Kaya you would say Ihnen.

c68e4835-4ac3-4cc6-9372-3b67f4a09daf: Frau (woman) is a female person, so the noun is feminine and takes **die**: **die Frau**.
fbc025da-31e9-44c1-9191-aab034a4e538: Mann (man) is a male person, so the noun is masculine and takes **der**: **der Mann**.
extra-a11-l05-01: Tafel is a feminine noun, so the definite article is **die**: **die Tafel**. Learn each noun with its article.
extra-a11-l05-02: Schere (scissors) is feminine and singular in German, so the article is **die**: **die Schere**. English "scissors" is plural, German is not.

extra-a11-l05-04: Stift (pen) is a masculine noun, so the definite article is **der**: **der Stift**.
extra-a11-l05-05: Tür (door) is a feminine noun, so the definite article is **die**: **die Tür**.

extra-a11-l05-08: First the notebook is new (ein Heft); now both speakers know which one, so the definite article follows. Heft is neuter: **das Heft**.

extra-a11-l05-14: Buch (book) is a neuter noun, so the definite article is **das**: **das Buch**.
extra-a11-l05-15: Kugelschreiber (ballpoint pen) is a masculine noun, so the definite article is **der**: **der Kugelschreiber**.
extra-a11-l05-16: Papier (paper) is a neuter noun, so the definite article is **das**: **das Papier**.
e0ac0425-9aea-44f8-8354-7c41cfbcb0d3: In the plural every noun takes **die**, whatever its singular gender: der Stuhl → **die Stühle**.
be8069b8-e189-4fa9-9888-c78e2d51736f: In the plural every noun takes **die**, even a neuter one: das Auto → **die Autos**.
88087bc2-73f6-5e32-a234-6674fcfff68e: Auto (car) is a neuter noun, so the definite article is **das**: **das Auto**.
1beeb08a-c03e-5ab8-8969-b3aec12ef2e5: Computer is a masculine noun, so the definite article is **der**: **der Computer**.
extra-a11-l05-06: Both speakers know which dictionary is meant, so the definite article is used. Wörterbuch is neuter: **das Wörterbuch**.
extra-a11-l05-09: The task wants the definite article for a known thing. Schere is feminine, so **die**: **Die Schere ist hier.**
extra-a11-l05-10: Bild is neuter, so **das Bild**. The subject comes first and the verb second: **Das Bild ist gelb.**
extra-a11-l05-12: Wohnung is a feminine noun (nouns ending in **-ung** are feminine), so the article is **die**: **Die Wohnung ist hier.**

extra-a11-l05-22: Papier is a neuter noun, so the definite article is **das**: **das Papier**.
extra-a11-l05-23: Schlüssel is masculine, so the article is **der**: **Der Schlüssel ist gelb.** Die is for feminine nouns and plurals.

1ce4f35f-6067-4fdf-a16b-689bb598fd67: Stuhl is masculine (der Stuhl). For something new or unknown, masculine takes **ein**: **ein Stuhl**. Eine is for feminine nouns only.

1ed2c78f-8f65-52e3-9e63-97f2a5b0663b: After sein, a job takes no article in German: **Ich bin Lehrerin.** Never "eine Lehrerin" — that is the English habit ("a teacher").
f12e69ee-d9c6-54f1-a2e7-b93304d4713c: Computer is masculine (der Computer). After "Das ist" the masculine indefinite article is **ein**: **ein Computer**.

dd1c3d60-8ae7-4c94-8990-19633dcba36f: Mutter is feminine (die Mutter), so the pronoun is **sie**: **Sie ist meine Mutter.** The pronoun follows the article of the noun.
extra-a11-l03-01: The pronoun follows the article: der Bruder → **er**. So: **Er spricht Arabisch.**
extra-a11-l03-02: The pronoun follows the article: die Schwester → **sie**. So: **Sie spricht Deutsch.**

0ef58eff-0411-5dc0-9115-e607c9648f80: The speaker talks about themselves with **ich**; the matching form of sein is **bin**: **Ich bin hier.**
4299d5ca-a80e-5528-a6b9-0ac7bee052bb: For several people you address informally, the pronoun is **ihr**; the matching form of sein is **seid**: **Ihr seid meine Freunde.**

extra-a11-l03-05: Ana and I together means we, so the pronoun is **wir**: **Wir kommen aus Marokko.** Whenever "ich" is part of a group, use wir.
extra-a11-l03-06: Mein Vater is er. With sprechen the vowel changes in the er-form: e becomes i, **er spricht**. Not "sprecht".
extra-a11-l03-07: Subject first, verb second. After **wir** the verb ends in **-en**: **Wir kommen aus Marokko.**

898a0861-f041-509c-84ba-57bf2f027afb: After **ich** the verb takes **-e**: arbeit + e = **arbeite**. The extra e is only needed before -st and -t (du arbeitest, er arbeitet).
af4fc6ff-5616-5fb8-9ae3-6fa201d36fd3: After **ihr** (informal you, plural) the verb takes the ending **-t**: sag + t = **sagt**.

extra-a11-l08-18: Dienstag is a day of the week, so it takes **am**, not um: **Der Termin ist am Dienstag.** Um is only for clock times.
827c155d-7b87-53a3-b047-d53ab532f296: Everyday German uses the 12-hour clock and counts minutes past the hour with nach: 18:20 = **zwanzig nach sechs**.
ffb96fdf-5140-582a-bc5a-b3d17e131ea3: Official time uses the 24-hour clock with the word Uhr, so midnight is **null Uhr** (zero o'clock).

extra-a11-l08-07: Montag is a day of the week, so it takes **am**, not um: **Der Termin ist am Montag.** Um is only for clock times.
extra-a11-l08-08: Subject first, verb second, then the day and the time: **Der Termin ist am Dienstag um acht Uhr.** Day with **am**, clock time with **um**.
68be03d3-c547-41dc-9dc0-772fa974f74f: Haben is irregular; after **ich** the form is **habe**: **Ich habe ein Auto.** Hast is for du, hat for er/sie/es.

extra-a11-l09-03: Hunger is said with haben. After **wir** the form is **haben**, like the infinitive: **Wir haben Hunger.**

extra-a11-l09-04: Paul is er (he). After **er** the form of haben is **hat**: **Paul hat heute Suppe und Salat.**
extra-a11-l09-05: Ich möchte … (I would like …) is a fixed phrase for ordering. Subject first, then **möchte**, then what you want: **Ich möchte ein Glas Wasser.**

extra-a11-l09-08: After **ihr** (informal you, plural) the form of haben is **habt**: **Habt ihr Hunger?** The verb opens the yes/no question.
extra-a11-l09-09: Talking politely to the waiter, you use the formal you (Sie), which takes **haben**. The verb comes first: **Haben Sie auch Kuchen?**

extra-a11-l09-12: Der Kellner is er (he). After **er** the form of haben is **hat**: **Der Kellner hat Zeit.**

extra-a11-l09-16: Subject first, verb second. Die Kellnerin is sie (she), which takes **hat**: **Die Kellnerin hat Kuchen.**
dcfdd24d-b6da-4222-92a9-2e816bf4cc5d: Sein is irregular; after **ich** the form is **bin**: **Ich bin müde.** Bist is for du, ist for er/sie/es.
34957c67-c29b-43c9-b3ef-5346fa68fa52: After **er** the form of sein is **ist**: **Er ist Lehrer.** Note: no article before the job.
9fd52b13-6cb9-4430-b0b7-52d4a63c0a63: After **wir** the form of sein is **sind**: **Wir sind in Berlin.** Seid belongs to ihr.
da9e486f-2548-4462-9bdd-c59560ed7276: Das (that) is one thing, like er/sie/es, so sein takes **ist**: **Das ist gut.**
0fe8146d-6e90-4c1c-b127-618c44e456ba: After **du** (informal you) the form of sein is **bist**; in a yes/no question the verb comes first: **Bist du Student?**
extra-a11-l02-01: After **ich** the form of sein is **bin**: **Ich bin Studentin.** The job stands without an article.
extra-a11-l02-02: The formal you (Sie) takes **sind**, and the verb opens a yes/no question: **Sind Sie Lehrerin?**
extra-a11-l02-03: Mein Wohnort is one thing (er), so sein takes **ist**: **Mein Wohnort ist Bremen.**
extra-a11-l02-04: Meine Telefonnummer is one singular subject (sie), so sein takes **ist**: **Meine Telefonnummer ist …**
extra-a11-l02-05: After **ihr** (informal you, plural) the form of sein is **seid**; the verb opens the question: **Seid ihr acht Studenten?**
extra-a11-l02-13: Ana is a friend, so the informal you (du) is used. After **du** the form of sein is **bist**: **Bist du ledig?**
1e3a7370-9e9c-55ea-b513-496b45421861: Sie meaning they (plural) takes **sind**, the same form as wir: **Sie sind Kollegen.** Ist would be for sie meaning she.
19f1aa27-7634-5599-8a61-8f69e259f6d4: Das (that) counts like er/sie/es, so sein takes **ist**: **Das ist Kaffee.**
459b2960-6610-57b4-b4f9-631bf6eeed01: Sie meaning she (singular) takes **ist**, like er and das: **Sie ist meine Schwester.** Sind would be for sie meaning they.
extra-a11-l02-06: After **wir** the form of sein is **sind**: **Wir sind verheiratet.**
extra-a11-l02-07: After **ich** the form of sein is **bin**, and a job stands without an article: **Ich bin Lehrer von Beruf.** Never "ein Lehrer".
extra-a11-l02-08: After sein, a job takes no article in German: **Ich bin Lehrer.** "Ein Lehrer" copies the English "a teacher" and is wrong.
extra-a11-l02-14: Lena and Tim are addressed together as friends: ihr. After **ihr** the form of sein is **seid**: **Seid ihr Studenten?**
extra-a11-l02-15: Ana is one person (sie), so sein takes **ist**: **Ana ist Marokkanerin.** In a sentence the nationality is a noun; the form marokkanisch belongs on a form.
extra-a11-l02-16: In a sentence the nationality is a noun. For a man it is **Marokkaner**, for a woman Marokkanerin — like Student and Studentin.
extra-a11-l02-17: Subject first, verb second. After **ich** the verb kommen ends in **-e**: **Ich komme aus Marokko.** Aus answers "Woher?".
5c5c272b-ff81-5811-83b6-6e7fde71ba1b: Statement: Du bist müde. In a yes/no question the verb moves to position 1: **Bist du müde?** Bist is the du-form of sein.
d1777221-6b65-55c3-8ecd-dbaa0583db0c: Statement: Du hast Zeit. In a yes/no question the verb moves to position 1: **Hast du Zeit?** Hast is the du-form of haben.
426d0034-6957-500d-84d9-4c2844e5338c: Statement: Du kommst aus Polen. In a yes/no question the verb moves to position 1: **Kommst du aus Polen?** The du-ending -st stays.
8c1f7c82-1210-5d1b-8f48-8ad60f3cfa78: The stem arbeit- ends in -t, so the du-form adds an extra e: **arbeitest**. In a yes/no question it comes first: **Arbeitest du viel?**
14eac77e-603e-51e0-9a53-4e18fa5b9d8f: The formal you (Sie) uses the verb form **wohnen** (same as the infinitive). In a yes/no question it comes first: **Wohnen Sie in Berlin?**
e327c296-1ea8-51db-b3c5-a6409f00534c: The formal you (Sie) uses the form **sprechen** (same as the infinitive), placed first in a yes/no question: **Sprechen Sie Englisch?**
d58cff5b-760c-57bc-b030-05d1201f8846: Statement: Du trinkst gern Kaffee. In a yes/no question the verb moves to position 1: **Trinkst du gern Kaffee?**
a3ddac97-a8fb-5ddc-8a2d-3c7763e89667: Statement: Du kochst gern. In a yes/no question the verb moves to position 1: **Kochst du gern?** The du-ending -st stays.
ffec1d33-2826-5332-93e5-2b8efe7ece89: A short answer repeats the whole statement in the ich-form: **Ja, ich komme aus Italien.** "Ja, komme" has no subject, and "du kommst" talks about the wrong person.
extra-a11-l10-01: In a yes/no question the verb comes first, then the subject. Der Zug is er, and fahren changes its vowel: **Fährt der Zug nach Österreich?**
extra-a11-l10-02: Without a question word, the verb comes first and the subject second. Die Fahrkarte is sie, so **kostet**: **Kostet die Fahrkarte …?**
extra-a11-l10-03: In a yes/no question the form of sein comes first. Das takes **ist**: **Ist das Gleis vier?**
extra-a11-l10-04: In a yes/no question the verb comes first. After **du** the form of haben is **hast**: **Hast du eine Fahrkarte für morgen?**
extra-a11-l10-05: In a yes/no question the verb stands before the subject. Der Zug is er, so haben becomes **hat**: **Hat der Zug heute Verspätung?**
extra-a11-l10-06: Statement: Du fährst mit dem Bus. In the question the verb comes first: **Fährst du morgen mit dem Bus?** Fahren changes its vowel after du.
0b5c7d74-0e60-51b3-802e-50a4c8457f36: In a yes/no question the verb comes first and the subject second. Bist is the du-form of sein: **Bist du müde?**
e52a4dca-4065-58a0-ae8f-de107844d5f2: In a yes/no question the verb comes first, then the subject. After du the ending is -st: **Wohnst du in Köln?**
20edbc50-95ff-5914-9381-9673b2716b68: In a yes/no question the verb comes first, then the subject. After du the ending is -st: **Kommst du aus Polen?**
fa2176d8-3252-57b7-8e4e-0c009303f306: Mitkommen splits: in the yes/no question **kommst** comes first, du second, and the prefix **mit** goes to the very end: **Kommst du am Samstag mit?**
78abfd45-9be5-51ff-a294-12c1aa43d6e9: In a polite yes/no question the verb comes first and the formal you (Sie) second. Sie uses the form wohnen: **Wohnen Sie in Berlin?**
6f0fbd89-79de-53ab-9b82-67b4f5f734ed: In a polite yes/no question the verb comes first and the formal you (Sie) second. Sie uses the form haben: **Haben Sie Kinder?**
81cb7d4e-9f92-5d7a-a8a9-ac0a5302565e: A yes/no question starts with the verb: **Wohnst du in Köln?** The other three start with a question word (Wie, Wo, Wer) and ask for information.
extra-a11-l10-07: In a yes/no question the verb comes first, then the subject. After ihr the ending is -t: **Fahrt ihr mit dem Auto in die Schweiz?**
extra-a11-l10-08: In a polite yes/no question the verb comes first and the formal you (Sie) second. Sie uses the form fahren: **Fahren Sie morgen nach Deutschland?**
extra-a11-l10-09: Without a question word, the form of sein comes first, then the subject. Die Ankunft is singular, so **ist**: **Ist die Ankunft am Gleis vier?**
extra-a11-l10-10: Die Abfahrt is one thing (singular), so sein takes **ist**, not sind: **Ist die Abfahrt um neun Uhr?** Sind belongs to wir, sie (they) and Sie.
extra-a11-l10-11: The verb must match the subject. Der Fahrer is er, so haben becomes **hat**: **Hat der Fahrer Verspätung?** Haben belongs to plural subjects and Sie.
extra-a11-l10-12: In a yes/no question the verb comes first, then the subject. Der Bus is er, so the ending is -t: **Kommt der Bus zum Bahnhof?**
extra-a11-l10-13: In a yes/no question the verb comes first. Der Zug is er, so haben becomes **hat**: **Hat der Zug nach Österreich Verspätung?**
extra-a11-l10-14: In a yes/no question the verb comes first, then the subject. Die Fahrkarte is sie, so **kostet**: **Kostet die Fahrkarte nach Deutschland zwanzig Euro?**
extra-a11-l10-15: Without a question word, the form of sein opens the question. Die Abfahrt is singular, so **ist**: **Ist die Abfahrt vom Gleis vier?**
extra-a11-l10-16: A yes/no question starts with the verb. Der Bahnhof is er, so sein takes **ist**: **Ist der Bahnhof weit?**
extra-a11-l10-17: To turn a statement into a yes/no question, move the verb to position 1 and the subject after it: **Fährt der Zug nach Österreich?**
extra-a11-l10-18: The answer "Ja, der Zug hat Verspätung" repeats the statement. The question puts the verb first: **Hat der Zug Verspätung?**
extra-a11-l10-19: To turn a statement into a yes/no question, move the verb to position 1: Der Bus fährt … → **Fährt der Bus nach Deutschland?**
extra-a11-l10-20: The answer repeats the statement, so the question is the same words with the verb first: **Hat der Bus Verspätung?**
extra-a11-l10-21: To turn a statement into a yes/no question, move the verb to position 1 and the subject after it: **Fährt der Fahrer nach Österreich?**
extra-a11-l10-22: The answer "Ja, der Fahrer hat Zeit" repeats the statement. The question puts the verb first: **Hat der Fahrer Zeit?**
